Reggie Jackson was an outfielder and one of baseball's most dominant sluggers, best remembered for his dramatic postseason heroics—particularly his three home runs in Game Six of the nineteen seventy-seven World Series—that earned him the nickname Mister October. His five-season stint with the Yankees from nineteen seventy-seven to nineteen eighty-one revitalized the franchise and proved his ability to deliver under pressure.

Jackson hit three consecutive home runs in Game Six of the nineteen seventy-seven World Series off three different pitchers, cementing his legend as a clutch performer. He hit five hundred sixty-three career home runs, the fifth most at his retirement, with twenty-five hundred eighty-four hits; his postseason performance was proportionally even more dominant. Known as Mister October for his disproportionately great performances in October playoff baseball, Jackson played for the Yankees during their nineteen seventy-seven and nineteen seventy-eight back-to-back World Series championship run after a fifteen-year drought.

He had a combative but ultimately productive relationship with Yankees manager Billy Martin, creating tension and drama that captivated New York. A Hall of Fame first-ballot selection in nineteen ninety-three, his Yankees achievements were central to his legend. Derek Jeter is a later-era Yankees shortstop who would anchor the next dynasty. Don Mattingly was a Yankees contemporary who played alongside Jackson. Mariano Rivera was a pitcher from the Jeter-era Yankees who represented the next generation. Jackson saved the franchise through dramatic playoff performances.
